page: Microsoft Azure FX48-24mds_v2 is a specialized instance designed for workloads requiring extreme per-core compute performance coupled with massive memory capacity. Hosted on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor, the virtual machine provides 24 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 12 physical cores from an Intel Xeon 8573C processor running at 4.2 GHz. The x86_64 architecture incorporates 260 MB of L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets, including AVX-512, AMX tile, and AMX int8 matrix acceleration. The platform delivers 1008 GB of system memory, providing a substantial ratio of 42 GB of RAM per vCPU, and is equipped with 2832 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. It contains no hardware accelerators or GPUs.

Performance testing reflects strong compute velocity on single-threaded tasks. In Geekbench evaluations, the server achieves top-tier results in single-core compute and text processing, alongside upper-quartile scores in multi-core metrics and image processing. Single-threaded data throughput is reinforced by top-quartile performance in gzip compression and bzip3 decompression. Multi-core operations in stress-ng and PassMark sit firmly in the average tier relative to other high-core platforms, reflecting the 24-thread core ceiling, while memory bandwidth delivers 186.82 GB/sec on uncached large-block reads and 88.92 GB/sec on writes.

From an infrastructure efficiency perspective, the FX48-24mds_v2 offers a distinct advantage for workloads subject to per-core licensing constraints. By constraining physical core count while retaining a full 1008 GB memory pool, it maximizes resource density for memory-bound systems without incurring unnecessary software license costs. The tradeoff is reduced aggregate parallel throughput compared to instances offering higher vCPU counts. Consequently, this server is suitable for in-memory databases, electronic design automation (EDA), financial modeling, and large-scale data transformation pipelines requiring fast clock frequencies and extensive volatile memory.

Hardware provisions include 1008 GB of system RAM, yielding 42 GB per vCPU, along with 2832 GB of integrated local NVMe SSD storage and no discrete GPUs. The high memory-to-vCPU allocation allows organizations to optimize per-core commercial software licensing costs while handling massive datasets. This configuration is aligned with in-memory caching systems, electronic design automation, transactional databases, and large-scale analytics requiring rapid clock speeds and large memory allocations.
